items.title: Bifurcation, Loss of Hyderabad & the New Capital Amaravati
items.body:
### How bifurcation reshaped Andhra Pradesh

**In one line**
In 2014 the old Andhra Pradesh was split into two states, and the residuary AP lost its richest city (Hyderabad) while having to build a brand-new capital — the twin shock behind its money troubles ever since.

**Why it is asked**
The appointed day, the law, the asset-split ratio and 'why AP had no capital' are standard Prelims facts, and 'the economic cost of bifurcation' is a favourite Mains theme.

**The story**
Under the **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 (Act 6 of 2014)** — the President assented on **1 March 2014** and the split took effect (the 'appointed day') on **2 June 2014** — a new state of **Telangana** (10 districts, including **Hyderabad**) was carved out of the united state. Money, debts and assets were divided mainly in the **population ratio 58.32 : 41.68** (AP : Telangana).

The sting was that **Hyderabad** — the largest earner of taxes and the IT and services hub of the old state — went to Telangana. It was allowed to stay the **shared capital of both states for up to 10 years** (Section 5), but it was now Telangana's. Residuary AP was left with a **revenue deficit** (it earned less than it spent) and, crucially, **no capital city of its own**.

So AP chose a site for a **greenfield** (built-from-nothing) capital, **Amaravati**, on the **right bank of the Krishna river** in Guntur district, near Vijayawada. Instead of forcibly buying land, the government used a **Land Pooling Scheme**: farmers pooled their land voluntarily and were promised developed plots back. The capital region spans about 217 km², governed by **APCRDA**, and major works later drew World Bank and AIIB support.

**Picture it**

| Milestone | Detail |
|---|---|
| Assent to the Act | 1 March 2014 |
| Appointed day (split) | 2 June 2014 |
| Asset/liability ratio | 58.32 : 41.68 (AP : Telangana) |
| Hyderabad | Common capital for up to 10 years, then Telangana's |
| New AP capital | Amaravati, on the Krishna, Guntur district |

**Terms explained**
- **Appointed day** — the legally fixed date on which the new state came into being.
- **Residuary state** — the part left over after a new state is carved out (here, the new Andhra Pradesh).
- **Greenfield capital** — a city built from scratch on fresh land, not an existing city.
- **Land Pooling Scheme (LPS)** — farmers surrender land into a common pool and get back smaller developed plots instead of a cash price.
- **Revenue deficit** — when a government's day-to-day income falls short of its day-to-day spending.

**Don't confuse**
- The **assent date (1 March 2014)** is NOT the appointed day; the split happened on **2 June 2014**.
- The population ratio **58.32 : 41.68 favours AP** (the larger share), not Telangana.

**Remember it**
Appointed day = **2/6 (2 June) 2014**; the split ratio **58.32 : 41.68** leans to AP.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| AP Reorganisation Act 2014 | Split old AP; Telangana created on 2 June 2014 |
| Hyderabad | The rich capital went to Telangana (shared ≤10 years) |
| The twin shock | Lost revenue base AND had to build a new capital |
| Amaravati | Greenfield capital on the Krishna, via land pooling |
keyPoints: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (Act 6 of 2014): assent 1 Mar 2014, appointed day 2 Jun 2014; Telangana carved out.
Assets/liabilities split mainly on population ratio 58.32 : 41.68 (AP : Telangana).
Hyderabad went to Telangana but stayed common capital for a maximum of 10 years.
Amaravati is the greenfield capital on the Krishna's right bank in Guntur district, built via a Land Pooling Scheme.
Losing Hyderabad's revenue plus funding a new capital was the core post-bifurcation fiscal shock.
items.mnemonic: Appointed day = 2/6 (2 June) 2014; ratio 58.32:41.68 favours AP.

items.title: Macro Snapshot — GSDP, Growth, Per-capita & Sector Shares
items.body:
### The size and shape of AP's economy

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh is a large, fast-growing but still farm-heavy economy — roughly ₹19.75 lakh crore in size, growing 8-10% a year, yet carrying a stubborn deficit and debt left over from bifurcation.

**Why it is asked**
Examiners test the GSDP size and rank, the growth numbers, per-capita income versus India, and the three sector shares — often as data-based or match questions.

**The story**
Start with the **size**. AP's **Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP)** — the total value of everything the state produces in a year — is about **₹19.75 lakh crore (~US$205 billion) in 2026-27**, placing it roughly **8th-9th** among Indian states.

Now **growth**. AP's GSDP has grown **6.19% (2023-24), 8.21% (2024-25) and about 9.88% (2025-26)**, frequently beating the national rate (in 2024-25 real, constant-price growth was about 8% against India's ~6.5%; in Q2 of 2025-26 it grew ~11.28% against ~8.7% nationally). But totals say nothing about the average person, so we use **per-capita income** — GSDP divided by population. AP's figure rose to about **₹2.98 lakh (nominal) in 2024-25**, above the all-India ~₹2.35 lakh, yet its rank is only around **15th** (mid-table), because population is large.

Finally the **shape**. Split output into three sectors — agriculture, industry, services. AP's farm sector is unusually big (~37%), far above India's ~18%, yet **services are its single largest sector (~40%)** and their share keeps rising. That slow move from farms toward services and industry is called a **structural shift**.

The weak spot is **public finance**: AP carries a **public debt of about 35% of GSDP** and a persistent **revenue deficit**, the legacy of losing Hyderabad's revenues while spending on a new capital.

**AP Budget 2026-27 — the numbers asked**
Finance Minister **Payyavula Keshav** presented the budget on **14 February 2026**. Read the table as 'how big, how much borrowed, where the money goes'.

| Item (2026-27 BE) | Figure |
|---|---|
| Total expenditure (including debt repayment) | ₹3,32,205 crore (~₹3.32 lakh crore) |
| Net expenditure (excluding debt repayment) | ₹3,10,058 crore |
| Fiscal deficit / Revenue deficit / Primary deficit | 3.84% / 1.11% / 2.0% of GSDP |
| Capital outlay | ₹48,698 crore (+47%) |
| Highest single department | School Education (~₹32,308 crore) |
| NTR Bharosa pensions / Thalliki Vandanam / Annadata Sukhibhava | ₹27,719 cr / ₹8,456 cr / ₹6,600 cr |

New proposals in the same budget: an **AP Wealth Fund** (a state sovereign-wealth-type fund that manages and invests the state's financial assets); **free power to weavers** from 1 April 2026 — handloom weavers up to **200 units/month**, powerloom units up to **500 units/month**; and **Harita AP**, raising green cover from **30% (January 2026) to 37% by 2030** and 50% by 2047.

Two outside report cards: the **16th Finance Commission** gives AP a **4.22%** share of the divisible pool of central taxes for **2026-31**, and NITI Aayog's **Fiscal Health Index** ranks AP **17th of 18** major States (Punjab is last).

**Don't confuse (budget)**
- **₹3.32 lakh crore** is the *total* including debt repayment; **₹3.10 lakh crore** is net of it; ₹3.01 lakh crore is the 2025-26 revised total.
- **4.22%** is AP's Finance-Commission share — not its fiscal deficit (3.84%) or own-tax ratio.

**Picture it**

| Sector (GSVA, 2023-24) | Share |
|---|---|
| Agriculture & allied | ~37% |
| Industry | ~23% |
| Services (tertiary) | ~40% |

(On current-price 2024-25 figures the split is close to agriculture 37%, industry 21%, services 42%.)

**Terms explained**
- **GSDP** — Gross State Domestic Product, the state's total annual output.
- **Per-capita income** — total income divided by population, a rough measure of living standards.
- **Nominal (current prices)** — measured at today's prices, not adjusted for inflation.
- **Structural shift** — the gradual change in which sector (farms, industry, services) dominates an economy.
- **Revenue deficit** — day-to-day spending exceeding day-to-day income.

**Don't confuse**
- A **high GSDP rank (~8th-9th)** does not mean a high **per-capita rank (~15th)** — population drags the average down.
- AP being **more agrarian than India** does NOT mean farming is its largest sector — **services** are.

**Remember it**
'Big but farm-heavy': GSDP ~₹19.75 lakh cr, growth ~8-10%, services largest (~40%) but agriculture (~37%) double India's share.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| GSDP 2026-27 | ~₹19.75 lakh crore; rank ~8th-9th |
| Growth | 6.19% → 8.21% → ~9.88%, often above national |
| Per-capita (2024-25) | ~₹2.98 lakh (nominal); rank ~15th |
| Fiscal weak spot | Debt ~35% of GSDP; persistent revenue deficit |
keyPoints: GSDP 2026-27 ~₹19.75 lakh crore; national rank ~8th-9th.
GSDP growth: 6.19% (2023-24), 8.21% (2024-25), ~9.88% (2025-26) — often above national rate.
Per-capita income ~₹2.98 lakh nominal (2024-25); rank ~15th.
Sector shares 2023-24: agriculture ~37%, industry ~23%, services ~40%.
AP is more agrarian than India (national farm share ~18%) but services are its largest sector.
Public debt ~35% of GSDP (2025-26 est.) with a persistent revenue deficit.
items.source: MoSPI GSVA; AP Planning Dept; PRS AP Budget Analysis 2025-26 and 2026-27 (verified Sep 2026)

items.title: Primary-sector Strength — Rice Bowl, Aquaculture & Horticulture
items.body:
### Why farming, fish and fruit define AP

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh is India's 'Rice Bowl' and its number-one aquaculture state, with farming, fishing and horticulture together supporting most of its people.

**Why it is asked**
The 'Rice Bowl' tag, the Krishna-Godavari deltas, AP's No.1 rank in shrimp/fish, and Guntur chillies are recurring one-mark facts and the base for Mains answers on agrarian strength.

**The story**
AP earns its nickname the **"Rice Bowl of India"** from the fertile **Krishna and Godavari deltas**, where river water irrigates vast paddy fields. The state's four main rivers are the **Godavari, Krishna, Penna and Tungabhadra**. Even though agriculture's share of output is slowly falling, **about 60% of the population still depends on it**, so farm income carries huge social weight.

AP's biggest edge is in the **allied** activities. Using its long coastline and delta backwaters, it has become **India's leading aquaculture state**, producing the bulk of the country's **farmed shrimp** and a very large share of inland fish — a top foreign-exchange earner. AP is **India's largest producer of fish and shrimp**, with a large share of national output, and it **leads India in area under vannamei (whiteleg) shrimp culture**. In **horticulture** it is a leading producer of **chillies** (the Guntur region is famous worldwide), **mangoes** and citrus. Because horticulture is **climate-resilient and gives higher returns per hectare** than plain paddy, farmers have been voluntarily shifting toward it.

**Picture it**

| Strength | AP's position |
|---|---|
| Paddy / rice | 'Rice Bowl' via Krishna-Godavari deltas |
| Aquaculture (shrimp, fish) | India's No.1 producer and exporter |
| Horticulture | Leading in chillies (Guntur), mangoes, citrus |

**Terms explained**
- **Primary sector** — the part of the economy that extracts or grows natural produce: farming, fishing, mining.
- **Allied activities** — farm-linked sectors such as fisheries, animal husbandry and horticulture.
- **Aquaculture** — farming aquatic animals like shrimp and fish in ponds or backwaters.
- **Horticulture** — the cultivation of fruits, vegetables, flowers and spices (as opposed to staple grains).
- **Delta** — the fertile, flat land where a river splits and deposits silt before meeting the sea.

**Don't confuse**
- AP leads in **aquaculture and shrimp**, NOT in temperate crops like coffee, apples, tea or rubber (those are other states).
- A **falling GVA share** of agriculture does not mean fewer people depend on it — about 60% still do.

**Remember it**
'Rice, shrimp, chilli' — paddy from the deltas, No.1 shrimp from the coast, and Guntur chillies lead horticulture.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Rice Bowl | Krishna-Godavari deltas make AP a top paddy state |
| Rivers | Godavari, Krishna, Penna, Tungabhadra |
| Aquaculture | India's No.1 in farmed shrimp and inland fish |
| Horticulture | Guntur chillies, mangoes, citrus — high-return crops |
keyPoints: AP = 'Rice Bowl of India'; Krishna and Godavari deltas anchor paddy.
Four main rivers: Godavari, Krishna, Penna, Tungabhadra; ~60% of people depend on agriculture.
AP is India's leading aquaculture state — dominant in farmed shrimp and inland fish exports.
Horticulture leader: Guntur chillies, mangoes, citrus; climate-resilient and high-return.
Allied sectors (fisheries, horticulture) increasingly drive farm-sector value.
items.source: AP Socio-Economic data; fisheries & horticulture depts (verified Sep 2026)

items.title: Water Resources, River Boards & the Polavaram National Project
items.body:
### Water: AP's lifeline and its biggest dispute

**In one line**
Because AP's wealth grows out of river water, bifurcation turned the Krishna and Godavari into shared assets managed by two boards, and made the giant Polavaram dam its most important project.

**Why it is asked**
The two river boards and their headquarters, Polavaram's 'National Project' status under Section 90, and its 960 MW / 23-lakh-acre figures are classic Prelims and the spine of water-themed Mains answers.

**The story**
When a state is split, its rivers do not stop flowing across the new border — so the Act set up two referee bodies under an **Apex Council** chaired by the Union Water (Jal Shakti) Minister: the **Krishna River Management Board (headquartered in AP)** and the **Godavari River Management Board (headquartered in Telangana)**. Even so, **sharing the Krishna and Godavari waters remains a live AP-Telangana dispute**, and the Krishna tribunal's term was extended to settle project-wise shares.

The centrepiece is **Polavaram**, a dam on the **Godavari** in Eluru/Polavaram district. The Act declared it a **National Project under Section 90**, meaning the **Centre funds and executes** it and Telangana's consent is treated as already given. Polavaram is **multipurpose**: it is designed to irrigate about **23 lakh acres**, generate **960 MW** of hydel power (12 units × 80 MW), and supply drinking water, holding roughly **194 tmcft** of water and transferring some Godavari water into the Krishna basin. Its engineering — a deep underground **diaphragm wall** beneath an earth-and-rock dam, plus a large river diversion — makes it one of India's most complex dams; it is advanced but not yet complete.

**Picture it**

| Board | Headquarters |
|---|---|
| Krishna River Management Board | Andhra Pradesh |
| Godavari River Management Board | Telangana |

**Terms explained**
- **River Management Board** — a central body that oversees sharing and operation of a shared inter-state river.
- **Apex Council** — the top body (Union Water Minister + both Chief Ministers) that settles disputes between the two boards.
- **National Project** — a project the Centre funds and prioritises, usually meeting most of its cost.
- **Multipurpose project** — one dam serving several goals at once: irrigation, power and drinking water.
- **tmcft** — 'thousand million cubic feet', a unit for measuring large volumes of stored water.

**Don't confuse**
- **Krishna Board sits in AP; Godavari Board sits in Telangana** — easy to reverse.
- Polavaram is on the **Godavari**, not the Krishna, even though it sends water toward the Krishna.

**Remember it**
Boards swap neatly: **Krishna → AP, Godavari → Telangana** (K before G, AP before TS alphabetically).

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Two boards | Krishna (HQ AP), Godavari (HQ Telangana), under an Apex Council |
| Polavaram | National Project (Sec 90) on the Godavari; Centre executes |
| Benefits | ~23 lakh acres irrigation, 960 MW hydel, drinking water |
| Status | Advanced but incomplete; a continuing AP-Telangana water issue |
keyPoints: Krishna Board HQ in AP; Godavari Board HQ in Telangana; both under an Apex Council (Union Water Minister).
Polavaram is on the Godavari (Eluru district), declared a National Project under Sec 90 of the Act.
Multipurpose: ~23 lakh acres irrigation, 960 MW hydel (12 x 80 MW), drinking water; ~194 tmcft storage.
Centre executes Polavaram; Telangana's consent is deemed given under Sec 90.
Krishna-Godavari water-sharing is a continuing AP-Telangana dispute.
items.mnemonic: Boards swap intuitively: Krishna->AP, Godavari->Telangana (K before G, AP before TS alphabetically).
items.source: AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (Sec 84-90); Polavaram Project Authority/APGENCO (verified Sep 2026)

items.title: Industry, Ports, Visakhapatnam & the VCIC Corridor
items.body:
### AP's coast as an industrial engine

**In one line**
Andhra Pradesh is turning its long coastline into growth — with Visakhapatnam as its economic hub and the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor as India's first coastal industrial corridor.

**Why it is asked**
The second-longest-coastline fact, Vizag as the lone major port and economic hub, and the VCIC/East Coast Economic Corridor are frequent Prelims items and anchor Mains answers on port-led growth.

**The story**
AP has **India's second-longest coastline (after Gujarat)** — about **974 km** — which is its biggest industrial advantage. A long coast means many ports, and ports pull in factories that want cheap export routes. AP's only **major (central-government) port** is **Visakhapatnam**; alongside it are **non-major** ports at **Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada and Machilipatnam**.

**Visakhapatnam (Vizag)** is the state's largest city and its commercial, IT and financial hub, home to a steel plant, the port and an IT SEZ at Rushikonda. It anchors the northern end of AP's flagship corridor.

That corridor is the **Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor (VCIC)** — the first phase of the **East Coast Economic Corridor (ECEC)**, which is **India's first coastal economic corridor**, supported by the Asian Development Bank. A corridor is a planned belt of industrial 'nodes' linked by good transport, so investment clusters instead of scattering. Its key nodes are **Visakhapatnam, Machilipatnam, Donakonda** and the **Chittoor/Srikalahasti-Yerpedu** area. The Reorganisation Act itself asked the Centre to examine a Vizag-Chennai corridor on the lines of the western Delhi-Mumbai corridor.

**Picture it**

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Coastline | ~974 km, 2nd longest after Gujarat |
| Major port | Visakhapatnam |
| Non-major ports | Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada, Machilipatnam |
| Flagship corridor | VCIC (first phase of the East Coast Economic Corridor) |

**Terms explained**
- **Major port** — a port run under the central government; AP's only one is Visakhapatnam.
- **Non-major port** — a port under the state (AP Maritime Board), such as Krishnapatnam or Gangavaram.
- **Industrial corridor** — a planned strip of connected industrial zones ('nodes') served by shared transport and utilities.
- **Node** — a designated industrial/urban growth point along a corridor.
- **SEZ (Special Economic Zone)** — an area with relaxed rules and tax breaks to attract export industry.

**Don't confuse**
- **Gujarat has the longest coastline; AP is second** — not the longest.
- The **VCIC** is on the east coast and is NOT the same as the western **Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor (DMIC)**.

**Remember it**
'Coast = capital': 2nd-longest coastline, Vizag as hub, and the VCIC as India's first coastal corridor.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Coastline | ~974 km, second only to Gujarat |
| Vizag | AP's largest city and economic/IT hub, lone major port |
| VCIC | First phase of the East Coast Economic Corridor, ADB-backed |
| Nodes | Visakhapatnam, Machilipatnam, Donakonda, Chittoor area |
keyPoints: AP has India's second-longest coastline (~974 km) after Gujarat; Visakhapatnam is its major port.
Non-major ports: Krishnapatnam, Gangavaram, Kakinada, Machilipatnam.
Visakhapatnam is AP's largest city and commercial/IT/financial hub.
VCIC is the first phase of the East Coast Economic Corridor — India's first coastal corridor, ADB-backed.
VCIC nodes: Visakhapatnam, Machilipatnam, Donakonda, Chittoor/Srikalahasti area.
items.source: AP Socio-Economic data; ADB VCIC/ECEC; AP Reorganisation Act 2014, 13th Schedule (verified Sep 2026)

items.title: Swarna Andhra Vision@2047, Regional Disparities, Districts & e-Governance
items.body:
### AP's long-term vision and its uneven map

**In one line**
AP wants to be a developed state by 2047, but its growth is uneven across regions, which is why the law promises a special package for its backward areas and the state leans on e-governance to deliver.

**Why it is asked**
The Vision@2047 tag, the three regions, the district-count timeline (13→26→28), the Special Category Status debate and MeeSeva are frequently tested facts.

**The story**
AP's headline ambition is **Swarna Andhra Vision@2047** ('Golden Andhra'), its long-term plan to become a **developed, high-per-capita economy by 2047**, timed to India's **Viksit Bharat@2047** and built on a **Public-Private-People (P4)** model where citizens join government and business as partners.

But the state's map is uneven. **Coastal Andhra** — the Krishna-Godavari deltas and Visakhapatnam — is relatively prosperous, while **Rayalaseema** (drought-prone, water-scarce) and **North Coastal Andhra (Uttarandhra)** lag on industry and incomes. Recognising this, **Section 46** of the Reorganisation Act directs a **special development package** for these backward regions.

To govern better, AP has repeatedly **redrawn its districts**: from 13 up to **26 on 4 April 2022**, and then to **28 from 31 December 2025**, adding **Polavaram** and **Markapuram**. For service delivery it runs **MeeSeva** ('at your service'), a single-window platform for online, time-bound citizen services such as certificates and payments.

One long-running grievance is the **Special Category Status (SCS)** demand. SCS was promised only as a **spoken assurance on the floor of the Rajya Sabha in February 2014**, not written into the Act; the Centre later offered a **Special Package** instead, and the dispute continues.

**Picture it**

| Stage | Districts |
|---|---|
| Before Apr 2022 | 13 |
| 4 April 2022 | 26 |
| From 31 December 2025 | 28 (added Polavaram, Markapuram) |

**Terms explained**
- **Viksit Bharat@2047** — India's goal of becoming a developed nation by its 2047 independence centenary.
- **P4 (Public-Private-People Partnership)** — a model adding citizens/community as a partner to the usual public-private pairing.
- **Special development package (Sec 46)** — extra central/state funds the Act promises for AP's backward regions.
- **Special Category Status (SCS)** — a status giving states higher central grants; AP was never formally granted it.
- **MeeSeva** — AP's single-window e-governance portal for citizen services.

**Don't confuse**
- **SCS was only a Rajya Sabha assurance**, NOT a clause in the Reorganisation Act — a very common trap.
- The relatively developed region is **Coastal Andhra**; the lagging ones are **Rayalaseema** and **North Coastal (Uttarandhra)**.

**Remember it**
'Golden by 2047, but uneven today': Vision@2047 (P4) up top, Rayalaseema and Uttarandhra at the bottom; districts 13→26→28.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Swarna Andhra Vision@2047 | Developed-state goal, Viksit-Bharat-aligned, P4 model |
| Lagging regions | Rayalaseema and North Coastal AP — special package (Sec 46) |
| Districts | 13 → 26 (2022) → 28 (from 31 Dec 2025) |
| SCS | A Rajya Sabha assurance, not in the Act; Special Package offered |
keyPoints: Swarna Andhra Vision@2047 = AP's long-term developed-state vision aligned with Viksit Bharat, using a P4 (Public-Private-People) model.
Coastal Andhra is developed; Rayalaseema and North Coastal AP lag and are named for a special package (Sec 46).
Districts: 13 -> 26 (Apr 2022) -> 28 (from 31 Dec 2025, adding Polavaram & Markapuram).
MeeSeva is AP's flagship integrated e-governance citizen-service platform.
Special Category Status was a Rajya Sabha assurance, not in the Act; a Special Package was offered instead.
items.source: Government of AP (Swarna Andhra Vision@2047, e-governance); AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (verified Sep 2026)

items.title: AP infrastructure — transport, energy & ICT
items.body:
### The three pillars that carry AP's growth

**In one line**
To replace what it lost with Hyderabad, AP is building growth on three infrastructure pillars — transport (ports, airports, rail, road), energy (thermal, hydro and fast-growing renewables), and ICT (fibre and digital governance).

**Why it is asked**
Port and airport names, the South Coast Railway headquarters, NH-16, Polavaram's 960 MW, and AP FiberNet/MeeSeva are high-frequency facts, and 'infrastructure as a growth driver' is a core Mains clause (M4-12).

**The story**
**Transport** comes first, built on AP's **~975 km coastline (second-longest)**. Operational ports include the central **Visakhapatnam Port** and non-major ports **Krishnapatnam** (Nellore), **Gangavaram** (a deep-water, ~21 m draft port near Vizag, now Adani-operated) and **Kakinada**; new greenfield ports under the **AP Maritime Board** are being developed at **Ramayapatnam** (Prakasam), **Machilipatnam** (Krishna) and Kakinada. In the air, AP's airports include **Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada (Gannavaram), Tirupati, Kurnool (Orvakal), Rajahmundry, Kadapa and Puttaparthi**, and the greenfield **Bhogapuram International Airport** (Vizianagaram district), officially named **Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport**, was **inaugurated in August 2026 (commercial operations from 17 August 2026)**, off **NH-16** near Visakhapatnam. On land, **NH-16 (Chennai-Kolkata, part of the Golden Quadrilateral)** is the arterial highway, and a dedicated railway zone — the **South Coast Railway (SCoR)** — became operational in **June 2026 with its headquarters at Visakhapatnam** (divisions: Guntakal, Guntur, Vijayawada, Visakhapatnam).

**Energy** is the second pillar: a mix of thermal (**Dr NTTPS, Vijayawada**; Krishnapatnam), hydro and a fast-rising share of **renewable energy**. AP is a leading solar and wind state and is building large **pumped-storage** and **green-hydrogen** projects, while **Polavaram** adds **960 MW** of hydel capacity.

**ICT** is the third pillar: **AP State FiberNet (APSFL / AP FiberNet)**, a **state-owned** network running since 2015, delivers broadband, IPTV and telephony to homes; **MeeSeva** (a single-window e-service platform) and the **Real Time Governance Society (RTGS)** — which supports **real-time monitoring and grievance handling** — power digital service delivery; and **Visakhapatnam** is promoted as the state's IT and executive hub, with IT investment clustering along the VCIC.

**Picture it**

| Pillar | Key assets |
|---|---|
| Transport | Vizag/Krishnapatnam/Gangavaram ports; Bhogapuram airport; SCoR rail; NH-16 |
| Energy | NTTPS thermal; Polavaram 960 MW hydel; solar/wind, pumped-storage, green H2 |
| ICT | AP FiberNet (APSFL); MeeSeva; RTGS; Vizag IT hub |

**Terms explained**
- **Major vs non-major port** — centrally run (Visakhapatnam) versus state-run (the rest).
- **Deep-water port** — one with enough draft (water depth, ~21 m at Gangavaram) to berth very large ships.
- **Railway zone** — an administrative division of Indian Railways; AP's own is South Coast Railway, HQ Visakhapatnam.
- **Pumped-storage** — a hydro method that stores energy by pumping water uphill and releasing it to generate power at peak demand.
- **IPTV** — television delivered over an internet/fibre network rather than cable or satellite.

**Don't confuse**
- The **South Coast Railway headquarters is Visakhapatnam, not Vijayawada** (Vijayawada is only a division) — a frequent trap.
- **Bhogapuram airport is now operational (from August 2026)** — it is no longer merely 'under construction'.

**Remember it**
Three pillars = **Transport, Energy, ICT**; SCoR HQ = **Visakhapatnam**; Bhogapuram = **Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport**.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Transport | ~975 km coast; Vizag major port; Bhogapuram airport live Aug 2026; SCoR HQ Vizag; NH-16 |
| Energy | Thermal + hydro + leading renewables; Polavaram adds 960 MW |
| ICT | AP FiberNet since 2015; MeeSeva & RTGS; Vizag IT hub |

Airports incl. greenfield Bhogapuram = Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport (Vizianagaram), inaugurated Aug 2026, off NH-16.
South Coast Railway (SCoR) zone operational from June 2026, HQ at Visakhapatnam; NH-16 is the arterial Golden-Quadrilateral highway.

ICT: AP FiberNet (APSFL, since 2015) broadband/IPTV; MeeSeva & RTGS digital services; Vizag as IT hub.
Infrastructure development spans transport, energy and ICT — central to AP’s growth.

items.title: AP flagship projects — Amaravati capital & Polavaram (status)
items.body:
### AP's two state-defining projects

**In one line**
Amaravati (the capital) and Polavaram (the irrigation dam) are the two giant projects that define post-bifurcation AP — one anchors administration and cities, the other water, power and farming.

**Why it is asked**
Their location, how they are funded, the 'three-capitals' episode, and Polavaram's National-Project status with its 960 MW / 23-lakh-acre figures are tested in both Prelims and Mains.

**The story**
**Amaravati** is AP's **greenfield capital**, in **Guntur district** on the **Krishna river**, about 15 km south-west of Vijayawada. It was built on land that farmers gave up under a **Land Pooling Scheme (LPS)** and planned by **APCRDA**. Its path was not smooth: between 2019 and 2024 the state floated a **'three-capitals'** idea (splitting capital functions across Visakhapatnam, Amaravati and Kurnool), which created uncertainty; this was later dropped, **Amaravati was reaffirmed as the sole capital**, and construction and funding (including **World Bank/ADB** support) resumed from 2024.

**Polavaram** is a **multipurpose National Project** on the **Godavari** in **Eluru/Polavaram district**, with the Centre funding the irrigation component. It is designed to irrigate about **23 lakh acres**, generate **960 MW** of hydel power and supply drinking water, and includes a **Godavari-Krishna link**. Its construction — the diaphragm wall and cofferdams — is **advanced but incomplete**, running on a revised timeline, and it is central to stabilising the delta.

Both are **capital-intensive, state-defining infrastructure**: Amaravati anchors administration and urban growth, while Polavaram anchors irrigation, power and water security.

**Picture it**

| Project | River / place | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Amaravati | Krishna, Guntur district | Greenfield capital |
| Polavaram | Godavari, Eluru district | Irrigation + 960 MW hydel + drinking water |

**Terms explained**
- **Greenfield capital** — a capital city built from scratch on new land.
- **Land Pooling Scheme (LPS)** — farmers pool land and receive developed plots back instead of cash.
- **APCRDA** — the Andhra Pradesh Capital Region Development Authority, which plans and builds Amaravati.
- **'Three-capitals' plan** — the 2019-24 proposal to spread capital functions across three cities, later shelved.
- **National Project** — a project the Centre prioritises and largely funds.

**Don't confuse**
- **Amaravati is on the Krishna**; **Polavaram is on the Godavari** — do not swap the rivers.
- The **'three-capitals' plan was dropped**; Amaravati is now the **single, reaffirmed capital**.

**Remember it**
Two giants: **Amaravati = Krishna, capital; Polavaram = Godavari, water and 960 MW power.**

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Amaravati | Greenfield capital on the Krishna; land-pooled; sole capital reaffirmed 2024 |
| Polavaram | National Project on the Godavari; Centre-funded irrigation |
| Polavaram scale | ~23 lakh acres, 960 MW hydel, drinking water; advanced but incomplete |
| Why they matter | Administration/urban growth (Amaravati) + water/power security (Polavaram) |
keyPoints: Amaravati: greenfield capital in Guntur dist. on the Krishna; built via farmers’ Land Pooling Scheme, planned by APCRDA.
Reaffirmed as AP’s sole capital; construction/funding (World Bank/ADB) resumed from 2024 after the ‘three-capitals’ phase.
Polavaram: multipurpose National Project on the Godavari (Eluru/Polavaram dist.); Centre funds irrigation.
Polavaram design: ~23 lakh acres irrigation, 960 MW hydel, drinking water, Godavari-Krishna link; advanced but incomplete.
Both are state-defining infrastructure — Amaravati for administration/urban growth, Polavaram for water/power security.

items.title: AP Budget 2026-27 by Sector, the Deficit Trend 2024-27 and AP's Budget Constraints
items.body:
**In one line:** AP's 2026-27 Budget of **₹3.32 lakh crore** puts about **42% into social services**, gives **welfare of weaker sections ₹52,855 crore**, and narrows the deficits after the **5.1% fiscal deficit of 2024-25** — but interest, pensions and salaries still leave little room.

**Why it is asked:** sector allocations, the deficit trend and "why AP's budget is tight" (Mains M4-3, M4-5) are standard AP economy questions.

## Sector allocations (2026-27 BE)

**The story**

| Sector / department | Allocation |
|---|---|
| **Welfare of SC, ST, OBC and minorities** (sector) | **₹52,855 crore** (+27%) |
| Education, sports, arts (sector) | ₹35,673 crore |
| **School Education** (highest single department) | **₹32,308 crore** |
| Rural Development | ₹20,610 crore |
| Health and Family Welfare | ₹19,630 crore |
| **Irrigation and Flood Control** | **₹16,734 crore** |
| Agriculture and Allied | ₹14,433 crore (+11%) |
| Energy | ₹14,120 crore |
| Urban Development | ₹12,541 crore |
| **Social services (total)** | **₹1.40 lakh crore — about 42%** of spending |
| Economic services (total) | ₹89,080 crore |

## Flagship project and scheme allocations

| Item | 2026-27 |
|---|---|
| **Polavaram dam** | **₹6,105 crore** |
| **Amaravati capital** | **₹6,000 crore** |
| NTR Bharosa pensions | ₹27,719 crore |
| Thalliki Vandanam | ₹8,456 crore |
| Annadata Sukhibhava | ₹6,600 crore |
| Rice subsidy | ₹3,344 crore |

## The deficit trend

| Year | Fiscal deficit | Revenue deficit | GSDP |
|---|---|---|---|
| **2024-25 (actuals)** | **5.1%** of GSDP | **3.8%** | ₹15,91,226 crore |
| **2025-26 (RE)** | 4.6% (₹80,567 crore) | **2.33%** (₹41,118 crore) | ₹17,62,357 crore |
| **2026-27 (BE)** | **3.84%** (₹75,868 crore) | **1.11%** (₹22,003 crore) | ₹19,75,073 crore |

- 2025-26 total spending (RE) was **₹3,00,535 crore**, below the ₹3,22,359 crore budgeted; capital outlay RE was only **₹33,135 crore**.
- **Primary deficit** 2026-27: **₹38,588 crore (2.0% of GSDP)**.

## Why AP's budget is tight (Mains M4-5)

1. **Committed spending** — interest (16% of revenue receipts), pensions and salaries take a big slice.
2. **Lost revenue base** — Hyderabad's taxes went to Telangana in 2014.
3. **Off-budget and guaranteed debt** — ₹1.28 lakh crore off-budget borrowing (CAG) and ₹1.77 lakh crore guarantees.
4. **Welfare commitments** — Super Six schemes and NTR Bharosa pensions.
5. **New capital and Polavaram** — two giant projects to fund at once.
- The **State Finance Commission** (Articles 243-I/243-Y) and the **AP FRBM Act, 2005** are the institutional checks.

**Don't confuse** — *School Education* (highest single **department**, ₹32,308 crore) with the *welfare of weaker sections* **sector** (₹52,855 crore); *2.33%* (2025-26 RE revenue deficit) with *1.11%* (2026-27 BE).

**TL;DR**
- AP 2026-27: welfare of SC/ST/OBC/minorities ₹52,855 crore (+27%); School Education the highest department at ₹32,308 crore.
- AP 2026-27: Irrigation and Flood Control ₹16,734 crore; Agriculture and Allied ₹14,433 crore; Health ₹19,630 crore; Rural Development ₹20,610 crore.
- Social services take about 42% (₹1.40 lakh crore) of AP's 2026-27 spending; economic services ₹89,080 crore.
- AP 2026-27: Polavaram dam ₹6,105 crore and Amaravati capital ₹6,000 crore; rice subsidy ₹3,344 crore.
- AP 2024-25 actuals: fiscal deficit 5.1% and revenue deficit 3.8% of GSDP; GSDP ₹15,91,226 crore.

items.title: AP Welfare — the "Super Six", NTR Bharosa, P4 and Swarna Andhra @2047
items.body:
**In one line:** the government elected in June 2024 replaced YSRCP-era schemes with its **"Super Six"** guarantees — **Thalliki Vandanam**, **Annadata Sukhibhava**, **Deepam-2**, **Stree Shakti** — raised **NTR Bharosa** pensions to **₹4,000 a month**, and frames everything inside the **Swarna Andhra @2047** vision and the **P4** zero-poverty model.

**Why it is asked:** the syllabus clause P1-C-5i names AP **welfare**; "which scheme replaced which", benefit amounts and the P4 terms are favourite AP questions.

## The welfare schemes

**The story**

| Scheme | Benefit | Replaced |
|---|---|---|
| **Thalliki Vandanam** | **₹15,000 a year per school-going child**, paid to the mother (launched June 2025) | **Amma Vodi** |
| **Annadata Sukhibhava** | **₹20,000 a year per farmer family** = ₹6,000 PM-KISAN + **₹14,000** from the State | **YSR Rythu Bharosa** |
| **Deepam-2** | **3 free LPG cylinders a year** to about 1.08 crore households | Deepam (upgraded) |
| **Stree Shakti** | **Free travel for women** in APSRTC non-AC buses from **15 August 2025** | — |
| **NTR Bharosa pensions** | **₹4,000 a month** (old age, widows, weavers, fisherfolk); **₹6,000** for the disabled; up to **₹15,000** for the bedridden | **YSR Pension Kanuka** |
| Matsyakara Bharosa | Support to fishermen during the fishing ban | — |

- In July 2026 Thalliki Vandanam credited about **₹10,121 crore** to **42.7 lakh mothers** for **67.5 lakh** students.

## The vision and the model

| Idea | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Swarna Andhra @2047** | Launched **November 2024** — a "wealthy, healthy, happy" AP by **2047**, built on **10 guiding principles ("Padi Sutralu")** such as zero poverty, jobs and water security |
| **P4 — Public-Private-People Partnership** | The richest **10% ("Margadarsis")** mentor and support the poorest **20% ("Bangaru Kutumbalu")**; target **zero poverty by 2029** |
| **Mana Mitra** | **WhatsApp governance** launched **30 January 2025**; scaled to **700 services** from 15 August 2025 |
| **RTGS** | Real Time Governance Society — dashboards and grievance tracking |

**Don't confuse** — *Thalliki Vandanam* (per child, to mothers) with *Annadata Sukhibhava* (per farmer family, includes PM-KISAN); *Margadarsis* (helpers, top 10%) with *Bangaru Kutumbalu* (helped, bottom 20%).

**Remember it:** "15-20-3-free-4000" — ₹15,000 per child, ₹20,000 per farmer, 3 cylinders, free bus, ₹4,000 pension.

**TL;DR**
- Thalliki Vandanam: ₹15,000 a year per school-going child paid to the mother (June 2025), replacing Amma Vodi.
- Annadata Sukhibhava: ₹20,000 a year per farmer family (₹6,000 PM-KISAN + ₹14,000 State), replacing YSR Rythu Bharosa.
- Deepam-2: three free LPG cylinders a year to about 1.08 crore households.
- Stree Shakti: free bus travel for women in APSRTC non-AC buses from 15 August 2025.
- NTR Bharosa pensions: ₹4,000 a month (₹6,000 disabled; up to ₹15,000 bedridden), replacing YSR Pension Kanuka.

items.title: AP Mega-Investments, Ports, Airport, Railway Zone and Amaravati Funding — Status in 2026
items.body:
**In one line:** 2025-26 brought AP its largest-ever investments — the **Google AI data hub at Visakhapatnam (~US$15 billion)**, the **AM/NS steel plant at Nakkapalli** and the **NTPC Green hydrogen hub** — while four new ports, **Bhogapuram airport (August 2026)** and the **South Coast Railway zone (June 2026)** came on stream and **World Bank–ADB money** restarted Amaravati.

**Why it is asked:** project → place → investment matching, "which is AP's 18th railway zone headquarters", Bhogapuram's name and the Amaravati funding partners are top AP current-economy items (M4-10, M4-12).

## Mega-investments

**The story**

| Project | Place | Size |
|---|---|---|
| **Google (with Adani, Airtel) AI data hub** | **Visakhapatnam** | About **US$15 billion (₹87,520 crore)** over 2026-30, **1 GW** — the largest single FDI in India |
| **ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel (AM/NS)** integrated plant | **Nakkapalli, Anakapalli** | **17.8 MTPA** planned (8.2 MTPA first); about **₹1.4 lakh crore**; foundation **23 March 2026**; output from 2029 |
| **NTPC Green hydrogen hub** | **Pudimadaka, Anakapalli** | About ₹1.85 lakh crore; foundation 8 January 2025 |
| Investment MoUs | Statewide | About **US$175 billion** across ~760 projects (claimed Feb 2026) |

## Ports — greenfield, under the AP Maritime Board

| Port | Status (2026) |
|---|---|
| **Ramayapatnam** | Over **80%** complete; first operations **December 2026** |
| **Mulapeta** (formerly Bhavanapadu, **Srikakulam**) | Over 57%; operations late 2026 |
| **Machilipatnam** (Krishna) | Over 57%; operations late 2026 |
| **Kakinada Gateway (SEZ) Port** | About 41%; target **March 2028** |

## Airport and railway zone

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Bhogapuram airport** | **Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport**, Vizianagaram district; inaugurated by the PM on **1 August 2026**; commercial flights from **17 August 2026**; Phase-1 about **₹4,592 crore** |
| **South Coast Railway** | India's **18th railway zone**; HQ **Visakhapatnam**; gazette **4 May 2026**; **operational 1 June 2026**; first GM **Sandeep Mathur**; divisions Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Guntur, Guntakal — a promise of the 2014 Act fulfilled |

## Amaravati — the funding revival

- **World Bank** and **ADB** committed **US$800 million each (US$1.6 billion)** for Phase-1; the World Bank's **Amaravati Integrated Urban Development Program** was approved on **19 December 2024**.
- The **Union Budget 2024-25** arranged **₹15,000 crore** through multilateral agencies for the capital.
- **APCRDA** implements; master plan **217 sq km** for about **3.5 million** people by **2050**; Phase-1 targeted around **2028**.

## Irrigation timelines

- **Polavaram** — works to finish by about **March 2027**, before the **Godavari Pushkaralu (2027)**; hydel units by early 2028.
- **Veligonda** (Prakasam, Krishna water from Srisailam) — Phase-1 directed to finish by July 2026.
- **Pattiseema lift (2015)** — the first project to link the Godavari to the Krishna, through the Polavaram right canal.

**Don't confuse** — *Bhogapuram* (Vizianagaram, named after **Alluri Sitarama Raju**) with *Gannavaram* (Vijayawada airport); *SCoR HQ Visakhapatnam* with *Vijayawada* (a division only).

**TL;DR**
- Google (with Adani, Airtel) AI data hub at Visakhapatnam: about US$15 billion (₹87,520 crore), 1 GW — the largest single FDI in India.
- AM/NS integrated steel plant at Nakkapalli (Anakapalli): 17.8 MTPA planned, about ₹1.4 lakh crore; foundation 23 March 2026.
- AP investment MoUs claimed: about US$175 billion across ~760 projects (Feb 2026).
- New ports: Ramayapatnam (>80%, ops December 2026), Mulapeta (Srikakulam) and Machilipatnam (>57%), Kakinada Gateway Port (target March 2028).
- Bhogapuram = Alluri Sitarama Raju International Airport: inaugurated 1 August 2026; flights from 17 August 2026; Phase-1 ₹4,592 crore.

items.title: AP Economy — Facts from Past Papers (Primary Share, Growth, Ease of Doing Business) and Related Concepts
items.body:
**In one line:** past APPSC and UPSC papers tested AP's primary-sector share (~30% in 2015-16), its high growth and farm dependence, its top ranks in **Ease of Doing Business**, and general ideas like the **Lorenz curve**, the **Bombay Plan** and **FDI-prohibited sectors**.

**Why it is asked:** these are the facts that already appeared in APPSC/UPSC questions on the AP economy — they tend to be repeated or paraphrased.

## AP economy in past papers

**The story**

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Primary sector share (2015-16)** | About **30%** of AP's GSDP (APPSC Panchayat Secretary 2016) |
| **Growth 2018-19** (Socio-Economic Survey) | GSDP growth **11.61%**; per-capita income **₹1,22,376** (+13.14%) |
| **Farm dependence** | Agriculture supports about **62%** of the people (survey reproduction) |
| **Ease of Doing Business** | AP topped the **DPIIT Business Reform Action Plan** state rankings — joint first with Telangana (2016), first in 2017-18 and **first in 2019** |
| **Hyderabad's loss** | The services-heavy Hyderabad region went to Telangana, so residuary AP became a **revenue-deficit** State |

## Infrastructure and farming items from UPSC

- **UPSC 2024:** among recent **greenfield** airports, **Donyi Polo (Itanagar)** and **Kushinagar** qualify — **Vijayawada (Gannavaram)** is an **expanded old airport, not greenfield**.
- **UPSC 2023:** **'Small Farmer Large Field'** — small and marginal farmers organise into groups and **synchronise their operations** to get economies of scale (a model piloted in AP).

## General concepts tested in AP economy papers

| Concept | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Lorenz curve** | Graph of **income inequality** (the Gini coefficient comes from it) |
| **Bombay Plan** | **1944** plan by leading industrialists (Tata, Birla and others) |
| **LPG** | Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation (1991) |
| **FDI prohibited** | **Chit funds**, **lottery**, **gambling and betting**, **Nidhi companies**, **atomic energy**, real-estate business, **tobacco cigars/cigarette manufacturing** |

**AP link:** AP's mix of high farm share and fast services growth is why APPSC asks both "primary-sector share" and "growth rate" questions about the same economy.

**Don't confuse** — *Vijayawada airport* (old, expanded) with *Bhogapuram* (true greenfield, opened 2026); *Lorenz curve* (inequality) with *Laffer curve* (tax rate and revenue).

**TL;DR**
- AP's primary sector contributed about 30% of GSDP in 2015-16 (APPSC 2016).
- AP Socio-Economic Survey: 2018-19 GSDP growth 11.61% and per-capita income ₹1,22,376; agriculture supports about 62% of people.
- AP topped the DPIIT Business Reform Action Plan ranking — joint first in 2016, first in 2017-18 and 2019.
- UPSC 2024: Donyi Polo and Kushinagar are greenfield airports; Vijayawada is not.
- UPSC 2023: Small Farmer Large Field — small farmers synchronise operations for scale.

items.title: For Mains — Andhra Pradesh Economy after Bifurcation
items.body:
### For Mains — resource mobilisation and growth in AP

Mains Paper-4 (clauses **M4-3** resource mobilisation in AP, **M4-5** AP budgeting/constraints, **M4-8** AP agriculture, **M4-10** AP industrial policy, **M4-12** AP infrastructure) and Paper-2 (**M2-10** bifurcation impacts) all draw on this subtopic. Frame answers around one thread: **bifurcation created a fiscal and institutional handicap that AP is trying to grow out of through resources, corridors and schemes.**

**Dimensions the examiner expects**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Causes / shock | Loss of Hyderabad revenue; no capital; revenue deficit; SCS denial |
| Resource base | Rice bowl, No.1 aquaculture, 2nd-longest coastline, renewable potential |
| Strategy | Amaravati, VCIC/ports, Polavaram, renewables, MeeSeva, Vision@2047 |

**Data points, reports and schemes to quote**
- Budget 2026-27: total ₹3,32,205 cr; fiscal deficit 3.84%, revenue deficit 1.11% of GSDP; capital outlay ₹48,698 cr (+47%).

**Use in answers**
- **Example:** cite the Google-Adani Vizag data hub and ArcelorMittal-Nippon steel plant as evidence that port-led, corridor-driven FDI is replacing lost Hyderabad revenue.
- **Quote:** frame bifurcation through the Act's own promise of a 'special development package' (Sec 46) for backward regions versus the unfulfilled Special Category Status assurance.
